title: Saving energy with light? Experimental studies assessing the impact of colour temperature on thermal comfort
research_question: To test whether the colour temperature of illumination (realised through manipulating the ceiling light) impacts on thermal comfort, based on the hypothesis that a lower colour temperature is associated with feeling warmer and a higher colour temperature with feeling cooler.

participants.description: Study 1: N=32 (18 male, 14 female), mean age 25.5 (SD 4.8) for 2700K and 23.9 (SD 3.5) for 6500K. Study 2: N=32 (23 female, 9 male), mean age 23.9 (SD 3.0) for 2700K and 22.9 (SD 1.9) for 6500K. Age range 18-35 years.
participants.recruitment: Participants were recruited through the subject pool of University College London (UCL).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Climate chamber with LED-based lighting system (ChromaWhite) set to either 2700 K (warm, yellowish-reddish light, 550 lux) or 6500 K (cold, bluish light, 495 lux). Ambient air temperature continuously changed from 24°C to 20°C (cooling cycle) or 20°C to 24°C (warming cycle) over 60 minutes. Relative humidity kept at 50%, air velocity below 0.1 m/s.

ASHRAE standard scale (5-point: Perfectly bearable (1) to Unbearable (5))

mechanisms: hue-heat hypothesis (psychological association of warm colours with warmth/cold colours with coolness)
psychological adaptation (habituation and expectation altering reaction to sensory stimuli)
physiological effect (e.g., via metabolic rate, melanopsin-containing receptors) - though the authors argue against this for their specific findings
implementation_implications: Dynamically tuning the colours of lighting using LED technology may prove to be a tool for energy reduction in buildings by decreasing the energy needed for cooling and heating.
Being able to turn off air conditioning or heating without compromising comfort would be of benefit for grid stability.
Offer 'warm' and 'cool' zones in offices where people could choose to sit depending on their preference.

limitations: The study tested only a narrow temperature range.
Only two light settings were tested in a highly controlled environment.
The sample was limited in the age range tested (18-35 years).
Participants did not perform demanding tasks and were under no time pressure, which might limit generalizability to real-world settings where task engagement is high.
Multiple other sources of light (e.g., displays, daylight) in real workplaces were not accounted for.
Variability in the light colour field due to vision wandering might mask effects in real-world settings.
The temporal stability of the light effect on comfort needs to be tested, as it might wear off after prolonged exposure.
It needs to be established that differentially coloured illumination does not negatively impact mood or performance.
Further research is needed to test if estimates of room temperatures (as opposed to comfort perceptions) are not affected by colour.
The survey questions used in Study 1 might be inadequate for assessing thermal comfort in dynamically changing conditions.
The sample of males in Study 2 was very small (N=4 and 5, respectively) for gender effects.
The analysis of temperature at first clothing change in Study 2 excluded participants who did not put on any clothing, making it problematic.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Psychological/Non-visual effects of light on thermal perception
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Illumination colour temperature can influence perceived thermal comfort and sensation beyond its direct radiant heat contribution, through psychological associations or non-visual physiological pathways.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates how the psychological association of colour temperature (warm vs. cool light) influences subjective thermal perception.
